samples: The editors' introduction argues that The Lord of the Rings, though written by a philologist rather than a philosopher, dramatizes perennial questions Tolkien cared about as a Catholic: whether power always corrupts, whether death can be a gift, and the tension of fate versus free will. It frames the volume's method by invoking Socrates, who drew on art, sport, and music his listeners already knew to provoke examination of their lives, presenting Tolkien's fiction as the same kind of popular-culture doorway into the great questions.

Eric Katz reads the One Ring as a variation on Plato's Ring of Gyges from the Republic: both grant impunity, and both pose the question of whether anyone would stay moral if able to act without consequence. Where Plato only argues that unchecked power corrupts the soul, Tolkien shows it through Gollum's ruin, Boromir's fall, and Frodo's final failure at the Cracks of Doom, while Galadriel, Bombadil, and Sam refuse the Ring by knowing who they are. Katz concludes Tolkien answers Plato's 'why be moral?' with 'to be yourself.'

Theodore Schick treats the Rings of Power as an allegory-free meditation on externalized 'potency,' applying it to emerging genetics, nanotechnology, and robotics. He contrasts the Council of Elrond's choice to destroy the Ring with Boromir's wish to wield it, and with Bill Joy's call to relinquish dangerous research versus Drexler's promise that nanotech could end poverty and disease. Schick argues our situation differs from Middle-earth because the knowledge cannot be un-forged, so grassroots social taming, not destruction of a single artifact, is the realistic response to knowledge-enabled mass destruction.

Alison Milbank reads the One Ring as a fetish in both Freud's sexual sense (an object severed from the whole, twice literally cut from a finger, warding off the castrating maternal power figured in Shelob) and Marx's economic sense (a commodity that estranges makers from things and reduces persons to hoarders like Smaug). Against fetishism she sets Tolkien's gift-economy, embodied by Bombadil tossing the Ring in the air and by Sam's elvish rope, and Heidegger's older sense of the 'thing' as a gathering, so the novel teaches us to receive the world back as gift rather than possession.

Gregory Bassham mines the happy communities of the Shire, Rivendell, and Lothlorien for six keys to happiness: delight in simple things (linked to Epicurus's natural pleasures and Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles, close friendship (grounded in Aristotle's claim that friendship is the greatest external good), good character, cherishing beauty and creativity, and recovering wonder. He argues Tolkien's hobbits and elves illustrate what modern happiness research confirms, so Tolkien functions as a philosophical guide to a more joy-filled life.

Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum, two hobbits of shared nature and culture who both pursue happiness but reach opposite ends. Gollum's happiness is possession of the Precious, a thing, sought in isolation and won by murdering Deagol, which destroys him; Sam's happiness is fellowship in the Shire with Frodo and Rosie, and his love for Frodo lets him surrender the Ring where Gollum cannot. Drawing on Aristotle's tie between happiness, one's nature, and friendship, Gracia concludes that for ordinary beings happiness is achievable only in a social context whose key is love expressed as loyalty and sharing.

book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
samples: The introduction argues that Doctor Who and philosophy share a common origin in wonder (quoting Plato's Socrates and Aristotle) and traces the show's shifting worldview across the eleven Doctors. It claims early Who embodied Enlightenment 'positivism' (the pro-science Hartnell/Pertwee eras) but that the post-1996 and post-2005 series turned toward Romanticism and Sartrean/de Beauvoirian existentialism, framing the surviving Doctor's post-Time War 'angst,' homelessness and burden of freedom through existentialist themes.

This chapter reads the Doctor as poised between positivism and phenomenology. It uses Hume's Fork and the Vienna Circle's verificationism (via 'The Daemons' and 'Tomb of the Cybermen') to cast the pro-science Doctor as an empiricist, then argues he is equally a Husserlian phenomenologist attentive to the 'life-world' and a Heideggerian Dasein whose time-travelling homelessness and the show's sense of the uncanny (unheimlich) embody being-in-the-world, thrownness and the flight from the worldhood of the world.

Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.

Focused on the 'Monstrous Other' and the 'base under siege' story, the chapter uses Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition and Sartre's 'the look' to read Cybermen, the Flood ('Waters of Mars') and the Silurians as Others through which humans define themselves, with Levinas on the face and history. Its final section frames the Doctor and the Master as Gothic doubles of love and strife, using Spinoza's monism, principle of sufficient reason and conatus to argue the power-hungry Master paradoxically fits Spinoza's system better than the order-imposing 'Dark Doctor.'

This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.

On regeneration and personal identity, the chapter runs Doctor Who through Leibniz's law of identity and soul-based individuation, Locke's memory criterion of personhood, and Hume's bundle theory, testing them against multi-Doctor stories, the Ganger duplicates ('The Almost People'), 'The Girl Who Waited' (closest-continuer theory) and 'City of Death.' It then shifts to physicalism (the Morbius brain) and to a pragmatist, social theory of the self (James, Dewey, Mead's 'taking the attitude of the other,' Dennett's intentional stance), reading the reintegration of identity in 'The Doctor Dances.'

This composite chapter opens with the volume's Introduction and then runs several essays. Jeff McLaughlin's 'What If?' reads DC's Crisis on Infinite Earths and Marvel's What If? series as literal illustrations of Leibniz's possible-worlds metaphysics: the multiverse of Earth-1, Earth-2 and the 3,000 doomed universes dramatizes counterfactuals and Leibniz's Theodicy argument (via the principle of sufficient reason) that God actualizes only the best of infinitely many possible worlds, with Descartes invoked on why a perfect God permits imperfection. Amy Kiste Nyberg's essay analyzes the 1954 Senate hearings on EC horror comics (Gaines's 'The Orphan') as an applied-ethics clash between publishers' free expression and protecting children, explicitly deploying Mill's On Liberty and harm principle to argue why the child-audience framing defeats the anti-censorship case. Stanford Carpenter's piece treats the Black Captain America (Truth: Red, White, and Black) as an epistemology-of-authorship problem.

This composite chapter argues philosophy through several comics. Jeremy Barris pairs Plato's dialogues with Amazing Spider-Man, using the allegory of the cave, the Forms, and Platonic love/eros to show that Spider-Man's bodily beauty, awkwardness, and self-trivializing irony draw readers toward goodness the way Plato says lust for beautiful bodies leads the soul upward to truth. Iain Thomson reads Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen as a 'deconstruction of the hero,' running Rorschach, Ozymandias and Dr. Manhattan through Nietzsche's Ubermensch and 'do not throw away the hero in your soul,' Heidegger's authentic 'choosing one's hero' and the uncanny, Kierkegaard's knight of faith, and Baudrillard's idea that an extreme realization destroys its own idea. Laura and Paul Canis read Daniel Clowes's Ghost World through Sartre's existentialism: Enid's post-high-school 'three o'clock' limbo enacts thrownness, abandonment, radical freedom and the flight from it into bad faith, contrasting Enid's authentic self-creation with Rebecca's settled conformity. Aldo Regalado's essay treats Tarzan, Superman, Captain America and the Black Panther as responses to modernity and race.

This file bundles three essays. Kevin de Laplante reads Paul Chadwick's Concrete story 'Stay Tuned for Pearl Harbor', treating Concrete's angry monologue about oil companies and overpopulation as enlightened anthropocentrism, while Maureen's silent reverie of merging her body with root systems and being 'raped' by bulldozers dramatizes Arne Naess's deep-ecological expanded self and an ecofeminist link between the oppression of nature-as-female and of women; the utilitarianism of Bentham and Mill and Leopold's 'think like a mountain' land ethic frame the anthropocentrism/nonanthropocentrism debate. Pierre Skilling reads The Adventures of Tintin through Montesquieu's and Aristotle's typologies of government, casting Marshal Kurvi-Tasch's Borduria as Arendt-style totalitarianism (a secret police as true executive, a bid for world domination) against the legitimate monarchy of King Muskar XII, whose Syldavian sceptre works as a check on royal power. Terry Kading argues that 9/11 collapsed the superhero genre's binary of good versus evil into reality: bin Laden's 'monomaniacs' act as supervillains with a murky agenda, yet Spider-Man, Captain America and Superman comics concede no real superhero can rescue us, leaving only ordinary heroism and the compromised politics of national security.

book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
samples: William Irwin's introduction argues philosophy must engage popular culture rather than fear it as Plato feared Homer and the poets. He invokes Plato's allegory of the cave to make the case that the philosopher who has left the cave must return and 'learn to see the shadows again'—use The Simpsons, The Matrix and Seinfeld as the vernacular through which prisoners can be led out—and answers Adorno-style culture-industry worries that mass entertainment is mere opiate. He closes by echoing Aristotle's serious treatment of the popular art (tragedy) of his day as warrant for treating today's pop culture philosophically.

Carolyn Korsmeyer uses Aristotle's Poetics dictum that the 'probable impossible' beats the possible improbable to argue popular narrative can actually conduct philosophy, not merely illustrate it. Her central case is that the TV series Angel—the ensouled, guilt-cursed vampire who concludes 'if nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do'—independently arrives at the same existentialist position as Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity, with no textual borrowing. She contrasts The Matrix's dramatically sustained Cartesian dream-doubt against the 'improbable impossible' Dallas dream-season, showing why one is a philosophical vehicle and the other bankrupt.

Irwin asks 'what is popular culture?', rejecting Noel Carroll's 'mass art' accessibility criterion (using the Sex Pistols, Slipknot and the Beatles as counterexamples of inaccessible-yet-popular art) and Walter Benjamin's aura/mechanical-reproduction account, settling on popular culture as 'artifacts and subjects of mass interest and appreciation.' He rebuts Adorno's and Zizek's culture-industry charge that pop culture (e.g. The Matrix, The X-Files) ideologically ensnares audiences, and again deploys Plato's cave and the returning prisoner—citing Socrates meeting interlocutors where they are—to justify using pop culture as a bridge to philosophy while warning against 'abuse' (studying pop culture as philosophy).

Theodore Gracyk analyzes artistic allusion in mass art, arguing (against Carrier and partly with Carroll) that accessibility does not preclude esoteric interpretive richness. His signature case is that The Matrix's red/blue pill scene overtly alludes to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland yet covertly alludes to Lewis Carroll's Sylvie and Bruno lockets, foreshadowing Neo as a Christ figure who must 'love all.' Drawing on Paul Grice's conversational implicature and Austin's illocutionary/perlocutionary speech-act theory, he argues allusion (Alien/Star Wars, Randy Newman's 'I Love L.A.', the Deliverance banjo in The Simpsons) is intentional and normatively constrains which associations transfer from source to alluding text.

Noel Carroll examines how popular fictions bind audiences emotionally through their relation to characters, starting from Plato's claim in the Republic that the popular arts pander to the emotions (pity and fear). He rejects both 'identification' (we rarely share characters' states—we fear for lovers who feel bliss, feel joy when the villain is foiled) and the fashionable 'simulation' theory as comprehensive accounts, arguing instead that sympathy—a pro-attitude directed at morally endorsable protagonists like Maximus in Gladiator—is the real 'tie that binds,' supplemented by involuntary 'mirror reflexes' (mimicking a screaming face in horror films, tapping to Riverdance).

Ted Cohen denies there is any sound argument from 'X is better than Y' to 'it is better to like X,' using Bach vs. Elvis vs. Milton Babbitt on complexity to show the criterion collapses. He reframes art around 'communities of appreciation'—citing Augustine's claim that a people is defined by what it loves in common—and reports (via a blues club in Memphis and the Marriage of Figaro) that what all appreciators of a work share is 'nothing' but their love of it, a Goodman-style nominalism. He challenges Kant's insistence that genuine aesthetic judgments claim universality, arguing real appreciative communities are less-than-universal overlapping circles.

samples: William Young argues that South Park stands in the Socratic-Platonic tradition and that its critics repeat the charges (impiety, corrupting youth) that condemned Socrates in the Apology. Kyle and Stan's dialogues over euthanizing Stan's grandpa model Socratic questioning and thinking from others' perspectives, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty illustrates Arendt's banality of evil (Eichmann). Young adds a Freudian reading in which the show's vulgarity works like joke-telling to release repressed drives, so the crude cartoon actually serves the examined life.

Robert Arp uses South Park's cartoon Johnnie Cochran and his 'Chewbacca Defense' from 'Chef Aid' to teach basic logic: premises, conclusions, deductive versus inductive arguments, and validity/soundness versus strength/cogency. The Chewbacca Defense exemplifies the red-herring fallacy, and other episodes illustrate hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem. The chapter's subject is informal logic and fallacy theory rather than a single named philosopher or taxonomy concept.

David Kyle Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's 'wikiality' and 'truthiness' to attack individual and cultural relativism, arguing (via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany) that truth is not relative to persons or cultures. He deploys Locke's critique of 'enthusiasm' to show gut thinking is circular, and invokes Socratic admission of ignorance against the claim of a 'right to your opinion.' The upshot is a method: defend beliefs with argument, be agnostic when evidence is lacking.

Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.

Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.

Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.

samples: Engels argues that NBC's The Good Place, though premised on a merit-based afterlife, actually argues morality should not be grounded in afterlife reward. When Eleanor, Chidi, Jason, and Tahani learn the point system and can no longer earn points, they form the 'Soul Squad' to be virtuous for virtue's sake, echoing Aristotle's telos and Kant's claim that acting from fear of hell is a heteronomous, non-moral motive. She reads the unfair points system (no human admitted in 521 years) through Rawls's Veil of Ignorance and shifts the show toward rehabilitative justice, and treats the Good Place residents' boredom via Bernard Williams's tedium-of-immortality argument, with Chidi's 'wave returns to the ocean' speech mapped onto Hindu atman/Brahman and moksha.

Marinucci uses The Twilight Zone as a triple introduction to philosophy, the show, and the handbook, arguing that philosophy is defined not by necessary-and-sufficient conditions but by Wittgensteinian family resemblance and salient features (curiosity, depth, abstraction, controversy) learned through MacIntyre-style immersion in a practice. She reads episodes as thought experiments: the amnesiac astronaut in 'Where Is Everybody?' and living-doll/robot episodes echo Plato's cave and Descartes's Method of Doubt about appearance versus reality, Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' frames the problem of other minds, and episodes like 'The Shelter' and 'It's a Good Life' dramatize the tension between egoism and altruism and social conformity, including feminist gaslighting in 'Twenty Two.'

Pigliucci argues that Gene Roddenberry built an implicit argument for Stoicism into Star Trek's Spock, contra both the 'suppressed emotion / stiff upper lip' caricature and Farren's claim that Kirk is the truer Stoic. Reading Spock's talk of 'emotion' as the disruptive pathe and his 'logic' as the broad Stoic study of reason, he shows Spock embodying the dichotomy of control ('my legs, they're broken'), the four cardinal virtues, and Stoic cosmopolitanism aboard the Enterprise. Drawing on Brouwer's account of the sage, he tracks Spock's development from prokopton toward sagehood, cultivating eupatheiai like love and friendship (the Wrath of Khan sacrifice) and declaring 'logic is the beginning of wisdom, not the end.'

Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.

Eberl and Bishop read the reimagined Battlestar Galactica and Caprica through the biopolitics of Foucault and Agamben, tracing 'biopower' across four phases from Zoe Graystone's avatar to the arrival at Earth. They argue the show asks whether artificial Cylons are persons (Zoe's avatar exhibits Baker's first-person perspective and Buber's I-Thou recognition), and use Agamben's zoe/bios/'bare life' and Homo sacer plus Roslin's population control and abortion ban to show sovereign power over life. The Cylon occupation of New Caprica is read through Arendt's three stages of totalitarian dehumanization, and Lee Adama's plea to 'break the cycle' offers a fragile hope undercut by the finale's flash-forward to present-day robotics, showing humanity forgetting the lesson.

Jones argues that Starz's Black Sails, a Treasure Island prequel set in the Golden Age of Piracy, dramatizes social contract theory as non-hypothetical practice. Captain Flint's drive to make Nassau a sovereign pirate commonwealth ('I am your king') channels Hobbes's state of nature and irrepressible sovereign, while his choice to settle Nassau and belief that people can thrive if left free channels Locke; his eventual plan to install Silver and Madi as liked-and-feared leaders synthesizes the two. Jones maps the pirates' familial bonds onto Rousseau and their responses to injustice (Vane's gallows speech, the maroon alliance) onto Rawls's Veil of Ignorance, and reads pirate 'articles' and deposable captains as radical democracy and equality, complicated by manipulation, slavery, and tolerance.

samples: The author argues that Doctor Who functions as a 'great educator' that shapes viewers' reality and their conception of the good life, framing our birth into the world as being 'thrown' into a new environment we must assimilate. He applies Hegel's historical dialectic to the Doctor-versus-Daleks conflict, treating the Doctor (wisdom, liberty, compassion) and the Daleks (obedience, hatred, conquest) as opposing theses whose ongoing struggle synthesizes the wider universe's fear of the Daleks. Drawing on Carroll and Danesi, he claims pop culture like Doctor Who validates experience and creates collective structures of meaning, and that our chosen first Doctor becomes the interpretive framework through which we judge every later one.

The chapter casts the Doctor as a 'flâneur' who teaches an engaged, critical-thinking way of life, illustrated through episodes like 'Blink,' 'Heaven Sent,' and 'Kerblam!' where the Doctor (and viewer) solve mysteries through trial and error. It uses Hume and William James to argue the mind actively constructs reality into a narrative, and pairs the Doctor with Socrates as a truth-seeking 'midwife' teacher who withholds answers so companions can learn by living rather than being told. The Doctor's rejection of Time Lord non-interference models the Socratic examined life of engaging the world to know oneself and others.

The chapter weighs the Doctor's ethic of interference against the Time Lords' non-interference, using determinism and the 'butterfly effect' (Martha in 'The Shakespeare Code') to concede when disengaged observation is prudent, while insisting that non-interference fails to protect human dignity. Drawing on Terrence Des Pres's account of dignity as 'inward resistance,' and real-world dissidents Adam Michnik and Václav Havel's 'power of the powerless,' it reads 'Rosa,' 'The Woman Who Fell to Earth,' and the people of Le Chambon as models of dignified, communal resistance to wrongdoing. Citing Iris Young, it argues everyone bears moral responsibility to engage rather than remain a detached, complicit 'objective observer.'

The chapter runs the Doctor's regenerations and the 'Timeless Child' reveal through competing theories of personal identity: Plato's soul/Forms, Locke's memory continuity, and bodily continuity, all of which the Doctor's body-swaps and forgotten lifetimes defeat (the Twelfth Doctor's 'you are a broom' speech recasts the Ship of Theseus). It endorses an existentialist answer—personal identity is chosen and constantly 'becoming,' as the Thirteenth Doctor declares 'I know exactly who I am. I'm the Doctor'—and uses Sartre against Freud to explain how the Doctor and the Whovian fandom reconcile internal and external selves in a community of acceptance. It closes arguing that only an 'objective' immortality (memories preserved in the Matrix) survives death, not a subjective self.

The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

The chapter defines a 'moral monster' as one who delights in evil acts, arguing (via Jonathan Glover and Laurence Thomas) that Hitler-style evil is all-too-human, not alien. Using Hume's claim that action springs from passion, it contends the emotionless Cybermen are a mere force of nature (bad but not evil), whereas the Daleks, driven by hatred, tribalism, and a closed belief system, are genuinely evil monsters; the manipulating Master mirrors our everyday lying. It then examines retributive justice through Solomon's execution in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship' and 'A Town Called Mercy,' rejecting purely backward- or forward-looking punishment (citing Rawls on utilitarianism's injustice) in favor of the Doctor's needs-based, 'reprobative' punishment, mercy, and self-forgiveness over the Time War.
